note: F1: 'Required Practical Method' is AQA/Edexcel wording. OCR Twenty First Century Science uses Practical Activity Groups (this is PAG5).
F2: the effect of carbon dioxide concentration on the rate of photosynthesis is B3.1.4a, which is not bold, so it is assessed at both tiers.

find: Light intensity decreases with the square of the distance from the source: double the distance, quarter the intensity.
replace: (Higher tier) Light intensity decreases with the square of the distance from the source: double the distance, quarter the intensity.
note: F3: the inverse square law is B3.1.5, which is bold and therefore Higher tier only. The rest of this paragraph is B3.1.4a and is both-tier, so the paragraph must not be wrapped.

expect: A plant is kept in bright light with adequate water. The rate of photosynthesis stops increasing when more CO₂ is added but not when the temperature is raised. What was the limiting factor before CO₂ was added?
value: A plant is kept in bright light with adequate water. The rate of photosynthesis increases when more CO₂ is added, but not when the temperature is raised. What was the limiting factor before CO₂ was added?
note: F4: as written the stem says the rate does NOT rise when CO₂ is added, which rules out the keyed answer (carbon dioxide concentration). The stem now matches the key.

find: The living (biological) part is called the community; the non-living part is called the habitat.
replace: The living (biological) part is called the community; the non-living surroundings are the abiotic environment. A habitat is the place where a particular organism lives.
note: F7: a habitat is the place an organism lives, not the non-living part of an ecosystem. The non-living components are the abiotic factors (B3.4.1).

find: In UK grasslands, for example, red and grey squirrels compete for hazelnuts
replace: In UK woodlands, for example, red and grey squirrels compete for hazelnuts
note: F8: red and grey squirrels are woodland animals; the displacement of red squirrels happened in broadleaf woodland, not grassland.
F9: garbled drafting artefact — the instruction 'Define mutualism' was pasted into a question template.
F9: garbled drafting artefact — the instruction 'Define parasitism' was pasted into a question template.

find: This process — called <dfn class="term" data-def="The pollution of a water body by excess nutrients (especially nitrates and phosphates), leading to algal blooms, reduced oxygen levels and the death of aquatic organisms.">eutrophication</dfn> — triggers algal blooms
replace: The nutrient enrichment that follows is called <dfn class="term" data-def="The pollution of a water body by excess nutrients (especially nitrates and phosphates), leading to algal blooms, reduced oxygen levels and the death of aquatic organisms.">eutrophication</dfn>. It triggers algal blooms
note: F11: as written the name 'eutrophication' is attached to nitrate being washed out of the soil. Eutrophication is the nutrient enrichment of the water and what follows from it (B3.4 narrative).

find: Questions on the nitrogen cycle often test the names and roles of specific bacteria. Learn them as a sequence:
replace: This board names the carbon cycle and the water cycle, and asks about the role of microorganisms in cycling substances. The nitrogen cycle is a good example of that role. Learn it as a sequence:
note: F12: J257 lists carbon and water by name (B3.3.9, B3.3.10) plus the role of microorganisms (B3.3.11). Nitrifying and denitrifying bacteria appear nowhere in the spec, so the promise of questions on their names is not supported.

find: Name the four types of bacteria involved in the nitrogen cycle and state what each one converts. This is a common exam question — practise writing it out without any prompts.
replace: Name the three types of bacteria in the nitrogen cycle, plus the decomposers, and state what each one converts. Practise writing it out without any prompts.
note: F12/F13: removes the unsupported exam claim, and stops decomposers being counted as a fourth type of bacteria when the lesson itself says decomposers are bacteria and fungi.

find: The nitrogen cycle depends on four types of bacteria: nitrogen-fixing, nitrifying, denitrifying, and decomposing.
replace: The nitrogen cycle depends on nitrogen-fixing, nitrifying and denitrifying bacteria, plus decomposers (bacteria and fungi).
note: F13: contradicts the lesson's own text, which defines decomposers as bacteria AND fungi.
F14: the carbon cycle is B3.3.10, which is not bold, so it is assessed at both tiers.

expect: 1 mark: Joint presentation 1858; publication of On the Origin of Species 1859. (Award 1 mark for both dates correct.)
value: 1 mark: Joint presentation 1858; publication of On the Origin of Species 1859. Both dates are needed for the mark.
note: F15: 'Award 1 mark for' is a banned board rubric phrase; the house validator rejects the whole unit on it.
F16: the question gives no options, so labelling it multiple choice misleads the student about the format.
F17: speciation sits under B6.1.5, which is not bold, so it is assessed at both tiers.

find: stopping early leaves some susceptible bacteria alive, which then recover and multiply.
replace: stopping early can leave the least affected bacteria alive, and those are the ones most likely to carry resistance.
note: F18: the reasoning was inverted. Bacteria that are still susceptible surviving would not select for resistance; it is the least affected (partly resistant) cells that survive an incomplete course (B6.1.9).

find: and the domestic dog is Canis lupus familiaris
replace: and the domestic cat is Felis catus
note: F19: Canis lupus familiaris is a three-part subspecies name, so it contradicts the sentence teaching the two-part binomial system. Felis catus is a clean binomial.

find: roughly three-quarters of flowering plant species depend on animal pollinators to reproduce
replace: almost nine in ten flowering plant species depend on animal pollinators to reproduce
note: F20: about 87.5% of flowering plant species are animal-pollinated (Ollerton et al., 2011). The three-quarters figure belongs to leading food crop types, not to flowering plant species.

find: <dfn class="term" data-def="The variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within a particular ecosystem.">Biodiversity</dfn> is the variety of species found in a given area.
replace: <dfn class="term" data-def="The variety of life on Earth or in a particular area: the diversity of living organisms, the diversity of the genes they carry, and the diversity of ecosystems.">Biodiversity</dfn> is the variety of life in a given area. It has three parts: the diversity of living organisms, the diversity of the genes they carry, and the diversity of ecosystems.
note: F21: J257 defines biodiversity in B6.4 as organisms plus genes plus ecosystems. The species-only wording is the definition used by other boards.

expect: The variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within a particular ecosystem.
value: The variety of life on Earth or in a particular area: the diversity of living organisms, the diversity of the genes they carry, and the diversity of ecosystems.
note: F21: matches the corrected in-lesson definition (B6.4).

expect: The variety of all different species found in an area or on Earth.
value: The variety of life in an area: the diversity of organisms, the diversity of their genes, and the diversity of ecosystems.
note: F21: matches the corrected in-lesson definition (B6.4).

expect:
Which one of the following correctly defines biodiversity?
A) The number of individual organisms in a habitat
B) The variety of different species found in an area
C) The total mass of all organisms in an ecosystem
D) The rate at which new species evolve
value:
Which one of the following correctly defines biodiversity?
A) The number of individual organisms in a habitat
B) The variety of life in an area — its organisms, their genes and its ecosystems
C) The total mass of all organisms in an ecosystem
D) The rate at which new species evolve
note: F21: keeps the answer option consistent with the corrected definition.

expect: B) The variety of different species found in an area [1 mark]
value: B) The variety of life in an area — its organisms, their genes and its ecosystems [1 mark]
